# Uraga Sutta (Snp 1.1 (PTS Snp 1))
**ID:** Snp 1.1 (PTS Snp 1)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Uraga Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.1
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Uraga Sutta* ("The Snake", Snp 1.1) is the opening discourse of the *Uragavagga*, the first section of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994; SuttaCentral]. Composed entirely in verse using the Aupacchandasaka metre, the text comprises seventeen stanzas [Katre 1931; Norman 1983]. Each verse concludes with a regular rhetorical refrain: *so bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṁ / urago jiṇṇam iva tacaṁ purāṇaṁ* ("That monk leaves behind both the near shore and the far, as a snake sloughs off its old worn-out skin") [Katre 1931; Norman, Philological Approach; SuttaCentral]. The poem depicts a monastic who abandons emotional defilements, passion, doubt, and conditioned dualities to attain spiritual release [Norman 1983; Norman, Philological Approach; Nyanaponika Thera 1986].
That the *Uraga Sutta* originally circulated as an independent collection of verses is indicated by its presence in non-Theravādin traditions as a specific chapter (*Uragavarga*) within Dharmapada and Udānavarga literature [Norman 1983; Barua 1921]. SuttaCentral records parallels in the Patna Dharmapada (vv. 398–414), the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (vv. 51–90), Sanskrit and Tibetan recensions of the Udānavarga (chs. 18 and 30), Chinese versions (T 212.31, T 213.18, T 213.30), and Pali parallels in the Udāna (Ud 2.10) and Vinaya Khandhaka (Kd 17) [SuttaCentral]. Machine-computed matches from DharmaNexus confirm these findings, showing substantial cross-language reuse with the Patna Dharmapada, Tibetan Udānavarga (D0326 and D4099), Sanskrit Udānavarga, and Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99), as well as extensive internal reuse in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and *Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
In early Western Indology, the text was among the very first Pali canonical works printed in Europe, edited by Friedrich Spiegel in his 1845 *Anecdota Pâlica* [de Jong 1987; Harris 2006]. It was also translated into German by Ven. Nyanaponika Thera, who authored a dedicated commentary on its verses titled "The Worn-out Skin" [Nyanaponika Thera 1986].
